segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Para", this "for", "para", can also mean "in order to",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "in order to". So, in a sentence, for example:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "We have spoken in order to resolve it. We have spoken in order to resolve it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now in English we could just say: "We have spoken to resolve it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No? We don't need to say "in order to".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But whenever we have this "to"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: meaning "in order to",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: we want to translate this as "para" in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's make this sentence. First bit is: "We have spoken."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "We have spoken."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos hablado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hemos hablado. "To resolve it", "in order to resolve it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now "to resolve" is resolver. Ah? The same word, resolver.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So: "We have spoken in order to resolve it."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos hablado para resolverlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Hemos hablado para resolverlo. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, whilst the "to" of "to resolve", resolver, would fit nicely here,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I mean if we were to translate directly from English: "We have spoken to resolve it",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: it doesn't work in Spanish. Whenever this "to" means "in order to", we must put that para:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hemos hablado para resolverlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You could say: "We have spoken in order to try to resolve it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to try", related to intention?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intentar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "We have spoken in order to try to resolve it."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos hablado para intentar resol- resolverlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Hemos hablado para intentar resolverlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, only when the "to" implies "in order to", we want to put para.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The "to" form of the verb in Spanish is not enough to include that meaning; we must put para.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for example, if you want to say: "I'm here to see you."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Does it mean "I'm here in order to see you"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So: "I am here to see you.", informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy aquí para verte.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy aquí para verte.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is also something we could learn or interiorize through the negative language transfer

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: that some Spanish speakers make when they speak English.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, you might hear a Spanish speaker say: "I am here for see you" or "for seeing you".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might hear a Spanish speaker, especially with basic English, making this mistake.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, once you heard that a few times, you would say: "Oh,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: maybe this is how you say it in Spanish."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we don't want to forget this opportunity, the opportunity to learn from the negative language transfer,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: the mistakes that Spanish speakers make in English which originate from Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Once you hear the same mistake a few times, you can assume it probably comes from Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I have called you in order to speak about it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the first bit is "I have called you", "I have phoned", "I have called", informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He llamado... Ah, sorry. Te he llamado...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "...in order to speak about it."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...para hablarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: We don't use "about"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No. Good. Te he llamado para hablarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if we take the sentence in English: "I have called you to speak about it" and we translated directly,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: then we will say: "Te he llamado hablarlo."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But when that "to" means "in order to", we must put this para. Te he llamado para hablarlo. "I have called you in order to speak about it." Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to be" for states?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estar. And we said that we can use this to express when we are doing something right now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can say instead of "I eat", como, "I am eating", using this structure with estar and then the "-ing" form of the verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Do you remember how you would get the "-ing" form of comer, for example, of -er or -ir verbs?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comiendo? Comiendo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comiendo. Good. Comiendo. So we add on "-iendo" for -er, -ir verbs. And for -ar verbs we add on...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: "-ando".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say: "I am eating"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy comiendo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy comiendo. And this means right now, no? "I am speaking."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy hablando.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy hablando. "I am explaining it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To explain"... We would go from "explanation", but "explanation" is an exception; it's not explanación in Spanish as we might hope, it's

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: explicación.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we see we even have that "k" sound in explain, explicación.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We have it in English as well, in "inexplicable", for example, we say in English; inexplicable in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we can see where that sound's coming from. So how is "explanation" or "explication" in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Explicación.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And "to explain"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Explicar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Explicar. Good. So: "I'm explaining it" and you mean right now?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy explicándolo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy explicándolo. Lo estoy explicando. The lo can go on the end of a "to" form,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but it can also go on the end of one of these "-ando" or "-iendo" forms as well, so you have the option: lo estoy explicando, estoy explicándolo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you mean right now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Actually, in explicar, we get this plicar from plicare that we mentioned before, meaning "to fold"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: in Latin, so explicar, "to explain", "to unfold".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might want to say: "I'm taking a Spanish course."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Even if you're not in the course right now in this moment, when we are taking a course in our minds,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: there's a period of time in which we are taking a course, and when we say it, we're in that period of time.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If I say "I'm taking a Spanish course", maybe I mean for 3 months and I'm in that period.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Do you remember what "to take" was? We used it with "to take a photo".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tomar. Tomar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tomar. So tomar, "to take". So: "I am taking..."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy tomando...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy tomando. "...a course"—I'm going to let you guess it.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Una corsa?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Close. It's not with A, it's with O.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un- un corso?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un curso, with a U. Curso. Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Curso.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "...of Spanish." This is how you would say "a Spanish course", "a course of Spanish".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un curso de español.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Estoy tomando un curso de español. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now what if we put this estoy in the past tense that we learned?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The past tense that is "-aba" or "-ía": "I was taking a Spanish course."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estar... estaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estaba tomando un curso de español.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estaba tomando un curso de español.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which means we actually have two ways of saying "I was taking".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can say estaba tomando, or we can just use tomar and use that that line in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would that sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tomaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. So both tomaba and estaba tomando mean "I was taking". So you have that option: estaba tomando un curso de español, or tomaba un curso de español. What was "to eat"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comer. Comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I was eating"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comía. Or how else could you say it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estaba comiendo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you have this option: comía or estaba comiendo. Most of the time they're interchangeable.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sometimes one might fit slightly better than the other, and it's something you will pick up very naturally when you're practicing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if in one situation people tend to use estaba comiendo rather than comía, you will pick it up.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have "-ando" and "-iendo" to form this "-ing".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we saw in Spanish that we don't use it after prepositions.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You don't use this "-ing" either if you say something like "Swimming is healthy" or "Running is healthy".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You don't use the "-ing" there either. You would just say: "To run is healthy. To swim is healthy."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you hear people toast in Spanish, you might hear them say ¡Salud!, which means "Health!"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Healthy" is saludable. "To dance is healthy."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Bailar es saludable.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Bailar es saludable. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To swim" is nadar. Nadar. "To swim is healthy."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nadar es saludable.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nadar es saludable.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we're seeing that we don't use the "-ing" in Spanish as much as we do in English.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sometimes in English, we make an adjective with "-ing".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We go from "to interest" to "interesting".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: When we do this in English, this "-ing" that we use in English to form an adjective,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: in Spanish, it's "-ante" for -ar verbs,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and "-ente" for -er, -ir verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for example, we had "to interest". What was "to interest"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Interesar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Interesar. So if you get rid of -ar and you put "-ante", you get that "-ing" adjective, "interesting". So how would you say "interesting"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Interesante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Interesante. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So when you make an adjective with "-ing" in English from the verb, you can just replace it with "-ante" or "-ente".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "to irritate" in Spanish, and you can go from "irritation"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Irritación... irritar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Irritar. So if you want to say "irritating"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Irritante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Irritante. Ah? "It is irritating."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es irritante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es irritante. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "to frustrate" in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Frustration... frustación... frustar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Frustrar. Frustrar. Yes, because you have the two R's, no? Fru-stra- frustra- Frustrar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Frustrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Frustrating"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Frustrante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Frustrante. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To wane", "to wane", to to reduce in size, in Spanish this is menguar. Menguar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Menguar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: When the moon gets smaller, it's waning. And "the moon" is la luna.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La luna.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La luna. So how would you say "the waning moon"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La luna menguante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So there we're making "waning" like an adjective, not like the verb, not menguando, ah? Menguante: la luna menguante.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Luna is an interesting word.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I don't know if you ever noticed like in English, Monday is "moon day". It's not very obvious in English

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: that the days of the week relate back to the planets, but in Spanish it's very obvious. You have la luna, the moon, and then you have lunes, Monday.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tuesday is martes, and Mars is Marte, planeta Marte.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Wednesday, in Spanish, is miércoles. What planet does that sound like?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mercury.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Jueves, in Spanish, is spelled with a J.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Jupiter.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Jupiter. Viernes is Friday.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Venus.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Venus. So you can see much clearer there how our days of the week are named after planets.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To live" was vivir, V-I-V-I-R.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So vivir is "to live".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vivir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We have two "to be"s. We have estar for states, and for characteristics, we have...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ser.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ser. And we said that un ser, un ser, means "a being", that we can use ser like a noun and we get "a being". So "a human being" is...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un ser humano.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un ser humano. You could also say "a living being", "a living being".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un ser vivir... vivo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you get this? How do you get... You could say un ser vivo. Vivo is also like an adjective which means "alive".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But "living", this adjective that we make with "-ing", we can build it from vivir. For -ar verbs we have "-ante", and for -er, -ir verbs, we have "-ente".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un ser viviente.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Un ser viviente, "a living being". What was "to go out" or "to leave"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To go out" or "to leave". So it's "to". I don't care if it's wrong, but I want it to end in -r.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, salir. Salir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salir. Now we have in English, you might have heard "salient", which means kind of protruding,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: or outstanding, or something that stands out, or sticks out, or protrudes. This is the Latin English version

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: of this "-ante", "-ente" rule, so we can see it even in English. How would "salient" be in Spanish? You can go from salient or you can go from salir.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Saliente.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Saliente. Good.
